final_text:
Two countries have sites: France and Italy.

The search for "Thomsen and Becker disease" with status Recruiting returned 9 trials. I counted a trial as interventional if its phase is listed as NA. I took the "-" entries to be observational, which I didn't confirm. Three trials met that test:

- **NCT06833489:** one site, in Marseille, France.
- **NCT07415837:** one site, in Clermont-Ferrand, France.
- **NCT07580365:** four sites, all in Italy. One of them is listed as suspended, not recruiting.

Two caveats:
- The search seems to match loosely. These three trials are listed under Becker muscular dystrophy, dystrophinopathy or rare muscle diseases, not myotonia congenita (Thomsen and Becker disease).
- I couldn't filter by study type directly, so the interventional label rests on the phase column.

<answer>{"answer": 2, "identifiers": ["NCT06833489", "NCT07415837", "NCT07580365"], "not_found": false, "confidence": 0.6}</answer>

Trial sites are listed in **23 distinct countries**. I got this from the 16 interventional trials with status Recruiting for "Von Willebrand disease" on ClinicalTrials.gov, by reading every site listed for each trial.

The countries are:
- **Americas:** United States, Canada, Colombia, Brazil
- **Europe:** Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, Switzerland, Austria, Ireland, Poland, Spain, United Kingdom, Georgia, Turkey
- **Asia and Pacific:** China, Japan, India, Australia
- **Africa:** South Africa

I counted a country if any site in a recruiting trial is listed there, whatever that site's own status. That includes a few sites marked Not Yet Recruiting or Completed. Turkey (NCT07575308), for example, appears only through not-yet-recruiting sites. Counting only sites that are themselves recruiting could give a lower number.

final_text:
Across the recruiting interventional trials I identified, sites are listed in 22 distinct countries.

I took the 11 trials with a listed phase as interventional: NCT07326592, NCT06049082, NCT06165341, NCT06996756, NCT07135427, NCT07227207, NCT05677971, NCT06405633, NCT06389877, NCT07431112 and NCT07555483. The tool has no study-type filter. I didn't check every trial without a phase. Of those, NCT06512454 and NCT07152834 appear observational, and NCT05335603 has no arms listed. The others, such as the registries and cohort studies, I assumed were observational.

The 22 countries are:
- **Americas:** United States, Canada, Brazil
- **Europe:** Austria, Belgium, Czechia, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Poland, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, United Kingdom
- **Asia-Pacific:** Australia, New Zealand
- **Other:** Georgia

I counted every country that has a site listed in any of those trials, whatever the individual site's status. Some of those sites are withdrawn, terminated, not yet recruiting or active but not recruiting. Georgia appears only through withdrawn and terminated sites in NCT07431112. Finland appears only through an active, not recruiting site in NCT06405633. If you want only countries with a site that is currently recruiting, the count would be lower, and I haven't worked out that number.

final_text:
Trial sites are listed in **26 distinct countries** across the 34 interventional trials for Duchenne muscular dystrophy with Recruiting status on ClinicalTrials.gov (as of 2026-11-06).

I found the 34 trials with a Recruiting status filter and an interventional-only study-type filter. I then pulled the site list for each trial and counted the distinct countries.

The countries are: United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Italy, Belgium, France, Spain, Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Sweden, Czechia, Hungary, Romania, Slovenia, Serbia, Belarus, Russia, Georgia, Turkey, Israel, Egypt, Pakistan, China, Australia and New Zealand.

- **Which sites count:** I counted every country listed on a Recruiting trial, including sites whose own status is not recruiting. Examples are not-yet-recruiting, active-not-recruiting, completed and withdrawn sites. If you counted only sites that are themselves recruiting, the total would be lower. Czechia, Hungary, Slovenia, Egypt, Israel, Serbia and Sweden appear only through such sites.
- **Trials that aren't strictly drug trials:** The interventional filter also returned some device, behavioral and diagnostic studies that list Duchenne muscular dystrophy among their conditions. I kept them in.

# trial

## Commands

- `get trial <nct_id>` - protocol card by NCT ID
- `get trial <nct_id> eligibility` - show registry-supplied eligibility criteria and CTGov document availability
- `--json get trial <nct_id> documents` - standalone CTGov posted-document manifest
- `get trial <nct_id> document <filename>` - exact advertised raw bytes with no PDF conversion (32 MiB maximum)
- `get trial <nct_id> locations` - site locations section
- `get trial <nct_id> --offset <N> --limit <N> locations` - paged location slice
- `get trial <nct_id> outcomes` - primary/secondary outcomes
- `get trial <nct_id> arms` - arm/intervention details
- `get trial <nct_id> references` - trial publication references
- `get trial <nct_id> all` - include every ordinary section
- `search trial [filters]` - search ClinicalTrials.gov (default) or NCI CTS (`--source nci`)

## Useful filters (ctgov)

- `--condition <name>` (or `-c`)
- `--intervention <name>` (or `-i`)
- `--no-alias-expand`
- `--status <status>` (or `-s`)
- `--phase <NA|1|1/2|2|2/3|3|4>` (or `-p`); named `PHASEn` and Roman forms are accepted
- `--facility <name>`
- `--age <years>` (finite 0-150; decimals accepted, e.g. `0.5`)
- `--sex <female|male|all>`
- `--mutation <text>` - broadly searches CTGov title, summary, eligibility, and keywords. After broad discovery, simple mutation text is checked against registry eligibility to remove exclusion-only matches; trials where the term is absent remain discoverable, while boolean expressions are discovery-only.
- `--criteria <text>`
- `--biomarker <text>` - phrase search over keyword, intervention, and condition on CTGov; prefer for gene-level broadening when `--mutation` is too specific.
- `--sponsor-type <nih|industry|fed|other>`
- `--prior-therapies <text>`
- `--progression-on <drug>`
- `--line-of-therapy <1L|2L|3L+>`
- `--lat <N>` (finite -90 to 90) + `--lon <N>` (finite -180 to 180) + `--distance <miles>`
- `--results-available`
- `--has-results` (alias)
- `--study-type <interventional|observational|...>`
- `--date-from <YYYY-MM-DD> --date-to <YYYY-MM-DD>`
- `--count-only`
- `--limit <N> --offset <N>`

## Phase values

- Scalars: `NA`/`N/A`; `EARLY_PHASE1`/`early_phase1`/`early1`; `PHASE1`/`1`/`I` through `PHASE4`/`4`/`IV`.
- Combined: `PHASE1/PHASE2`/`1/2`/`I_II` and `PHASE2/PHASE3`/`2/3`/`II_III`.
- Matching is case-insensitive. A combined value is one combined provider label, not an OR search.

## CTGov alias expansion

- `--condition` sends the supplied condition literally.
- Every `--intervention` worker is sent to CTGov as one quoted literal.
- `--intervention` auto-expands known aliases selected by a trial-safe policy: plausible trade names and investigational codes are included, while systematic chemical synonyms are excluded.
- Expanded rows add `Matched Intervention` in markdown and `matched_intervention_label` in JSON when an alternate alias matched first.
- A rejected expanded alias does not discard successful requested-name results, but leaves the exact total unknown.
- `--no-alias-expand` performs one literal request for the supplied name.
- `--next-page` is not supported when intervention alias expansion fans out to multiple queries; use `--offset` or `--no-alias-expand`.

## Posted CTGov documents

- Use the BioMCP retrieval handle from `documents`; filenames must match the current manifest exactly.
- Eligibility remains registry-supplied text. Posted documents may contain additional detail but do not guarantee that any criterion is resolved.
- Document forms are CTGov-only, standalone, and excluded from ordinary `all`.

## NCI source notes

- `--source nci --condition <name>` first tries to ground the name to an NCI disease ID and falls back to CTS `keyword`; there is no separate NCI keyword flag.
- `--source nci --status <status>` accepts one normalized status at a time and maps it to CTS recruitment or lifecycle filters.
- Combined inputs `PHASE1/PHASE2`, `1/2`, or `I_II` mean one Phase 1/2 label; `PHASE2/PHASE3`, `2/3`, or `II_III` mean one Phase 2/3 label, not an OR search.
- On NCI those combinations map to CTS `I_II` and `II_III`; scalar Roman `I` through `IV` map to the corresponding single phase. `--phase early_phase1` is not supported.
- `--source nci --lat/--lon/--distance` uses direct `sites.org_coordinates_*` CTS filters and serializes distance with the required `mi` suffix.
- NCI accepts one quoted value total across `--biomarker`, `--mutation`, and `--criteria`; it rejects repeated or combined values.
- NCI rejects CTGov-only `--study-type`, `--sponsor`, and update-date filters before making a request.

## JSON Output

- Non-empty `search trial --json` responses include `_meta.next_commands`.
- `get trial --json` can include CTGov source-provided intervention alternate names; See-also and JSON next commands may prefer search/article follow-ups for investigational codes.
- Alias-expanded trial rows may include `matched_intervention_label`.
- True zero-result filtered `search trial --json` responses include broadening commands in `_meta.next_commands`, such as loosening `--mutation`, widening `--distance`, relaxing `--status`, or trying `--biomarker`.
- The first follow-up drills the top result with `biomcp get trial <nct_id>`.
- `biomcp list trial` is always included so agents can inspect the full filter surface.

Trial sites for recruiting interventional "Poliomyelitis" trials are listed in 7 countries: Panama, China, the Philippines, Bangladesh, Ireland, Australia and the United States.

The ClinicalTrials.gov condition search returned 10 recruiting trials, and I read the site list for each one:

- **China:** NCT07354269 and NCT07891104.

- **Australia:** NCT07688369.
- **United States:** NCT05644522.

Two of the 10 are not polio-vaccine trials. NCT05663008 (Ireland) and NCT05644522 (United States) list post-polio syndrome among several conditions, and the search matched them on that. If you count only trials where poliomyelitis itself is the condition studied, you would lose Ireland and the United States and the answer would be 5. I counted all 10 because the search returned them for this condition.

final_text:
Trial sites for recruiting interventional chlamydia trachomatis trials are in 3 countries: the United States, Australia and Botswana.

The search returned 6 recruiting trials. I counted countries from the four that are interventional:

- **NCT07290439** (point-of-care STI testing, Emory): United States.
- **NCT06891417** (Sanofi mRNA vaccine, phase 1): Australia, with 7 sites.
- **NCT06428643** (seek, test and treat, Tulane): United States.
- **NCT07458802** (antenatal STI screening): Botswana.

I excluded the other two:

- **NCT07596316** (Antwerp, Belgium) is labelled observational in its record.
- **NCT06793605** (Hong Kong) looks observational from its title, "Community Burden of MG Infection". I did not confirm its study type, and it is mainly about Mycoplasma genitalium.

If both were counted anyway, the total would be 5, adding Belgium and Hong Kong.

final_text:
Four countries have sites in recruiting interventional trials from this search: Ethiopia, Iraq, Bolivia and Colombia.

The search for "cutaneous leishmaniasis" with status Recruiting returned 10 trials. Four of them are observational, so I excluded them: NCT00344188, NCT07783243, NCT06514560 and NCT07504757. Their sites were in the United States, Ethiopia, Ethiopia and Italy.

The six interventional trials and their sites:
- **Ethiopia:** NCT06746350 (Addis Ababa).
- **Iraq:** NCT06797544, NCT06798415 and NCT06798402 (all Baghdad).
- **Bolivia:** NCT06550609 (La Paz).
- **Colombia:** NCT06822478 (Medellín).

NCT06550609 is listed under mucosal leishmaniasis rather than cutaneous. The search returned it anyway. If you drop it, the count falls to 3 (Ethiopia, Iraq, Colombia).

I took the interventional or observational label from the study type shown on each record. I didn't check that field for the other six trials, which are the ones I counted as interventional.

Droxidopa is the only drug I found that fits, but I could not check it against Open Targets. The Open Targets lookup for multiple system atrophy (MSA) failed twice with a connection error. I built the candidate list from ClinicalTrials.gov phase 3 MSA trials instead, and I did not look up FDA labels or ANDA records. The label and generic status below come from my own knowledge.

- **Droxidopa:** It appears in the phase 3 MSA and neurogenic orthostatic hypotension trials (for example NCT00633880 and NCT02071459). Its label carries a boxed warning for supine hypertension, and generic droxidopa capsules have been approved through ANDAs.
- **Midodrine:** It has a boxed warning and US generics, so it would qualify if Open Targets lists it for MSA at phase 3 or later. I did not see it in the MSA trials I reviewed, so I left it out. This is the main uncertainty.
- **Other candidates:** Rifampicin, minocycline, and fludrocortisone have no boxed warning that applies here. Ampreloxetine and amlenetug are not marketed generics.

final_text:
Only amphotericin B meets both conditions. I could not pull Open Targets' phase 3+ drug list for visceral leishmaniasis through the tools, and I did not check Drugs@FDA or the FDA labels directly. This answer comes from my own knowledge of the drugs and their labels.

The drugs I would expect at phase 3 or later for this disease are amphotericin B (conventional and liposomal), miltefosine, paromomycin, pentamidine, and the antimonials (sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate). A search of ClinicalTrials.gov did return 13 phase 3 visceral leishmaniasis trials, which fits this set.

- **Amphotericin B (conventional):** It has a US generic (ANDA) and a boxed warning. The warning says to use it mainly for progressive, potentially life-threatening fungal infections and to verify the dose, because overdose can cause cardiopulmonary arrest. This is the only drug that meets both conditions.
- **Liposomal amphotericin B (AmBisome):** It has generics but no boxed warning.
- **Miltefosine (Impavido):** It has a boxed warning for embryo-fetal toxicity, but I know of no ANDA generic.
- **Paromomycin and pentamidine:** Neither has a boxed warning.
- **Antimonials:** They are not FDA-approved.

# visceral leishmaniasis

ID: MONDO:0005445

## Definition (MyDisease.info)

A severe form of leishmaniasis characterized by irregular bouts of fever, substantial weight loss, swelling of the spleen and liver, and anemia (which may be serious). If left untreated it may lead to death. Two species of Leishmania are known to give rise to the visceral form of the disease. The species commonly found in East Africa and the Indian subcontinent is L. donovani and the species found in Europe, North Africa, and Latin America is L. infantum, also known as L. chagasi. [https://www.who.int/leishmaniasis/visceral_leishmaniasis/en/, Wikipedia:Visceral_leishmaniasis]

final_text:
Three drugs fit: carboplatin, doxorubicin and etoposide. Only carboplatin's Open Targets phase and label were fully confirmed. Doxorubicin and etoposide each have an unconfirmed link, described below.

- **Carboplatin:** Open Targets lists Nephroblastoma at Phase 3. It has US generic ANDAs that are still marketed, such as Eugia, Hospira and Epic. Its FDA label carries a boxed warning for bone marrow suppression, vomiting and anaphylaxis.
- **Doxorubicin:** The Open Targets indication list was truncated, so I couldn't see a Wilms entry. I inferred it from seven Phase 3 Wilms trials that use doxorubicin. It has a boxed warning and US generics, which I know from the label but did not pull.
- **Etoposide:** Same gap as doxorubicin: the list was truncated and I didn't see a Wilms entry. The Phase 3 combination regimens include it, so I inferred it. I'm also relying on memory that its label has a boxed warning and that ANDAs exist.
- **Dactinomycin:** Excluded. It has marketed ANDAs, but its current label has no boxed warning.
- **Vincristine:** Excluded. Its label has a boxed warning, but every ANDA in Drugs@FDA shows as discontinued.
- **Cyclophosphamide:** Excluded because its label has no boxed warning. I'm going from memory here and did not pull the label.
- **Ifosfamide:** Excluded because I saw no Wilms entry in its Open Targets list.

# Wilms tumor

ID: MONDO:0006058

## Definition (MyDisease.info)

An embryonal neoplasm characterized by the presence of epithelial, mesenchymal, and blastema components. The vast majority of cases arise from the kidney. A small number of cases with morphologic features resembling Wilms tumor of the kidney have been reported arising from the ovary and the cervix. [NCIT:C3267]
Genes (Open Targets): WT1 (OT 0.850), GPC3 (OT 0.719), BRCA2 (OT 0.711), TRIM28 (OT 0.681), CTR9 (OT 0.584)

Wilms' tumor, Wilms' tumour

embryonal cancer (MONDO:0005564), mixed cell type cancer (MONDO:0005853)

# carboplatin - label, approvals
## FDA Label

### Boxed Warning
WARNINGS Carboplatin injection should be administered under the supervision of a qualified physician experienced in the use of cancer chemotherapeutic agents. Appropriate management of therapy and complications is possible only when adequate treatment facilities are readily available. Bone marrow suppression is dose related and may be severe, resulting in infection and/or bleeding. Anemia may be cumulative and may require transfusion support. Vomiting is another frequent drug related side effect. Anaphylactic-like reactions to carboplatin have been reported and may occur within minutes of carboplatin injection administration. Epinephrine, corticosteroids, and antihistamines have been employed to alleviate symptoms.
### Approved Indications
- the palliative treatment of patients with ovarian carcinoma recurrent

# vincristine sulfate - label, approvals
## FDA Label

### Boxed Warning
WARNINGS Caution–This preparation should be administered by individuals experienced in the administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection. It is extremely important that the intravenous needle or catheter be properly positioned before any vincristine is injected. Leakage into surrounding tissue during intravenous administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection may cause considerable irritation. If extravasation occurs, the injection should be discontinued immediately, and any remaining portion of the dose should then be introduced into another vein. Local injection of hyaluronidase and the application of moderate heat to the area of leakage help disperse the drug and are thought to minimize discomfort and the possibility of cellulitis. FOR INTRAVENOUS USE ONLY – FATAL IF GIVEN BY OTHER ROUTES. See OVERDOSAGE section for the treatment of patients given intrathecal Vincristine Sulfate Injection. WARNINGS This preparation is for intravenous use only. It should be administered by individuals experienced in the administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection. The intrathecal administration of Vincristine Sulfate Injection usually results in death. To reduce the potential for fatal medication errors due to incorrect route of administration, Vincristine Sulfate Injection should be diluted in a flexible plastic container and prominently labeled as indicated "FOR INTRAVENOUS USE ONLY – FATAL IF GIVEN BY OTHER ROUTES." See OVERDOSAGE section for the treatment of patients given intrathecal Vincristine Sulfate Injection.

The clinical trial search found NCT03086226, a phase 2 mycetoma trial. NCT01259336, a phase 4 itraconazole trial, turned up under "mycetoma" but is for pulmonary aspergillosis. Neither confirms the Open Targets entries.

Leflunomide is the only drug I could identify that meets both criteria, but I couldn't confirm it. The Open Targets disease query and the leflunomide label lookup both failed with "Connection closed" errors. I never saw Open Targets' list of drugs for this disease, so the candidate set comes from ClinicalTrials.gov trials.

- **Candidate drugs:** the phase 3 and 4 trials in IgG4-related disease involve inebilizumab, obexelimab, rilzabrutinib, belimumab, iguratimod, betamethasone (Diprospan), glucocorticoids and leflunomide.
- **Leflunomide:** the phase 4 trial NCT02703194 tests it for maintenance in IgG4-related sclerosing disease. From memory, its FDA label has a boxed warning (hepatotoxicity and embryo-fetal toxicity), and US generics exist under ANDAs. I didn't confirm either point with the tools.
- **The others don't qualify:**
  - Inebilizumab, obexelimab, rilzabrutinib and belimumab have no Drugs@FDA ANDA generics. Inebilizumab, obexelimab and belimumab are biologics, and rilzabrutinib is a new drug with no generics.
  - From memory, the corticosteroids (prednisolone, betamethasone) have no boxed warning.
  - Iguratimod isn't FDA-approved.

I didn't rule out other drugs Open Targets might list at phase 3 or later, such as azathioprine, mycophenolate or tacrolimus. They do carry boxed warnings and have generics, but I found no trial evidence that they reached phase 3 for this disease.

I found no drug that meets both conditions. This rests partly on my own recall, because the Open Targets disease lookup failed in this session. I couldn't pull the Open Targets list for human African trypanosomiasis (HAT) directly. The disease-section calls returned errors, and one command dropped the connection. I also did not query Drugs@FDA or the FDA labels.

Ketoconazole is the only drug that fits, but two points rest on my recall rather than on data I pulled.

- **Phase 3 or later in Open Targets:** The drug search for chromoblastomycosis (MONDO:0015908) returned only ketoconazole and posaconazole. I did not see the Open Targets phase for either drug directly. I'm assuming both reached phase 3 or later.
- **Marketed US generic:** Ketoconazole has oral tablet ANDAs in Drugs@FDA, for example Taro's ANDA075319 and Pharmazone's ANDA075912, both marked Prescription.
- **Boxed warning:** The label the tool returned was the topical cream, which has no boxed warning. Oral ketoconazole tablets carry a boxed warning for hepatotoxicity, QT prolongation and drug interactions. I'm going from memory on that, not from the retrieved label.
- **Posaconazole:** I excluded it because I recall its label has no boxed warning. I did not check that, or whether it has a marketed generic.
- **Itraconazole:** It has generic capsules and a boxed warning, but its Open Targets indications did not list chromoblastomycosis, so I left it out. That list may have been truncated.

ID: MONDO:0015908

## Definition (MyDisease.info)

Chromomycosis is a chronic cutaneous and subcutaneous fungal infection, found mainly in subtropical and tropical areas (in soil and plant debris and transmitted by traumatic inoculation), and characterized clinically by slow growing, verrucous nodules, squamous plaques, or chronic limited lesions which are most commonly found on the lower limbs and which are characterized histologically by the presence of muriform cells. It is caused by dematiaceous fungi, with the main etiological agents being Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Phialophora verrucosa and Cladophialophora carrionii. Rarely, it can be caused by Rhinocladiella aquaspersa. [Orphanet:182]

Warfarin and sacubitril/valsartan do have boxed warnings, but I couldn't confirm they are listed for Chagas in Open Targets, and the sacubitril/valsartan trials are for Chagas cardiomyopathy or heart failure.

Caplacizumab is the only approved drug I found acting on VWF that has no hereditary von Willebrand disease record. I couldn't confirm this against Open Targets directly, so it rests on indirect evidence.

- **Candidate list:** The VWF druggability table (DGIdb with Open Targets tractability) lists these approved drugs: caplacizumab, von Willebrand factor human, vonicog alfa, vitamin B6, factor VIII, methylene blue, phenylephrine and acetylcysteine. The `search drug --target VWF` command returned nothing, so the table was my only source for the list.
- **Not a candidate:** Von Willebrand factor human and vonicog alfa are von Willebrand disease replacement therapies, so they already have records for the disease.
- **Candidate:** Caplacizumab is an anti-VWF nanobody approved for acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura. I know of no hereditary von Willebrand disease indication or trial for it. A search of the clinical-trial registry for caplacizumab in von Willebrand disease failed with a connection error, so I didn't confirm that there.
- **Weaker links, not checked:** I left out vitamin B6, factor VIII, methylene blue, phenylephrine and acetylcysteine. Their links to VWF in DGIdb are weak, and I didn't check whether Open Targets counts them as VWF drugs. If it does, they would also lack a record for this disease and would belong on the list.

Open Targets has no clinical record linking any FGFR2 drug to X-linked intellectual disability, Cilliers type. A ClinicalTrials.gov search for "Cilliers" also returned no trials. So every approved FGFR2 drug is a naive repurposing candidate.

Seven of the eight drugs are approved:
- **Pemigatinib, futibatinib and infigratinib:** FGFR inhibitors, flagged as approved in the DGIdb/Open Targets druggability table.
- **Erdafitinib:** an FGFR inhibitor, approved.
- **Nintedanib:** a multi-kinase inhibitor, approved.
- **Palifermin:** a recombinant growth factor that acts on FGFR2b, approved.
- **Tasurgratinib:** approved in Japan (my recollection), which I did not confirm in the tools.

Lirafugratinib, the eighth drug, is not approved, so I left it out.

Three approved drugs act on PIK3CA and have no clinical record for macrodactyly of toes: inavolisib, gedatolisib and copanlisib. I did not confirm Open Targets' own evidence list for this disease. My exclusion of alpelisib rests on its PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum (PROS) indication, not on a direct check of its macrodactyly record.

- **Candidates:** a BioMCP search of drugs targeting PIK3CA returned alpelisib, inavolisib, gedatolisib, copanlisib, idelalisib, duvelisib, leniolisib and others still in development.
- **Excluded alpelisib:** Open Targets lists it for PROS, which is the disease family that includes macrodactyly, so it already has a clinical record.
- **Excluded idelalisib, duvelisib and leniolisib:** I assumed they act mainly on PI3Kδ (PIK3CD), and for duvelisib also PIK3CG, so I left them out as not really PIK3CA drugs. I did not check that assumption. BioMCP does list all three against PIK3CA, so these are the judgement calls.
- **Gedatolisib:** its brand name Revtorpyk suggests it is approved, but my Drugs@FDA lookup was for alpelisib only and returned nothing. I did not confirm gedatolisib's approval.
- **Copanlisib:** I included it from memory as an approved pan-class I PI3K inhibitor that hits PIK3CA. I did not check its approval status or its record for this disease.
- **Trial search:** a ClinicalTrials.gov search for macrodactyly returned only NCT05563831, a PROS evaluation that I did not open. I could not run the follow-up search for alpelisib in overgrowth because the connection closed.
